title: Format and types
summary:
This part fixes the exact type system the rewrite implements: the `.rmd` document and its YAML profile, frontmatter, the rich blocks and their fields, chart channels and options, data sources and the report folder, the `.rstyle.yaml` schema, diagnostics, report identity, and the CLI, MCP, HTTP, JavaScript and editor contracts. Rendered behaviour belongs to parts 04a–04d and visual choices to part 06; this part settles names, types, defaults, validation and failure modes. Current behaviour was read at `b4db233` (2026-10-16); evidence marked as reproduced was run with a release build on 2026-10-21 or 2026-10-22.

The decisions that change the most:

- **Style injection (TYP-51)**: a style file can put a live `<script>` into a report today; every CSS-bound value gets a closed grammar and every sink refuses unsafe characters.
- **Report identity (TYP-60, TYP-63, TYP-64, TYP-95, TYP-96)**: one ASCII slug function, a content hash over the whole publish request, a conflict error when a version is republished with different content, `latest` by SemVer, and permalinks that are never pruned. The last three reverse dec-73, today's deliberate publication-order `latest` and the June 50-version cap.
- **Checks in every host (TYP-15, TYP-94)**: missing fields and channels are caught by `validate` in every host, and one table says which operation runs which rule; generating every surface from one schema is ARC-09's decision (TYP-03).
- **Source order (TYP-25)**: tables, CSV downloads and payloads keep the author's column order.
- **Required description (TYP-07)**: publishing requires title, description and version, as S27-418 states.
- **Breaking changes to existing reports (TYP-83)**: `big` becomes `metric` (TYP-09), `suffix` becomes `unit` (TYP-16), currency formats go (TYP-87), `line.smoothing` goes (TYP-17), header-image and style aliases go (TYP-06, TYP-52), camelCase chart style keys become kebab-case (TYP-50), and image `title` and media `alt` move (TYP-29 to TYP-31). Ten of the eleven golden inputs INT-55 names use at least one (all but hello-world); each break fails with a diagnostic that names the fix, and one migration rewrites them (INT-51).

Decide together with: ARC-08 (TYP-53, diagnostic record), ARC-09 (TYP-03), ARC-10 (TYP-69, MCP inputs), ARC-12 (TYP-51, serializer), ARC-14 (TYP-32, blocked embeds), ARC-21 (TYP-63, TYP-64, TYP-96), ARC-34 (TYP-41), ARC-36 (TYP-75, TYP-97), INT-13 (TYP-13), INT-36 and OPN-04 (TYP-67), INT-51 and INT-55 (TYP-83), OPN-39 (dec-18 in TYP-44, dec-65 in TYP-53, dec-73 in TYP-63), and the part 04b cards that add or remove fields (FEA-RP-03 to FEA-RP-05, FEA-RP-12 to FEA-RP-14, FEA-RP-20, FEA-RP-21, FEA-RP-33).

Answer each card: **accept** keeps the proposal as the rewrite's rule, **edit** replaces it with your text, **reject** drops it from the rewrite, and **defer** leaves it open. Items under Pending format extensions apply only if part 04d keeps the feature. Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

items.title: The `.rmd` document
items.question: Is this the complete document model: optional YAML frontmatter, a CommonMark body, and tagged YAML fences that become rich blocks?
items.why: Every host, the spec and the generated schema derive from this model; anything outside it is ordinary Markdown or an error.
items.proposed:
A report is one UTF-8 `.rmd` file of at most 16 MiB; a leading BOM is dropped.

| Part | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Frontmatter | Optional YAML mapping. It starts only when line 1 is `---` and ends at the next `---` or `...` line. |
| Unclosed frontmatter | `frontmatter.unclosed` (warning) at line 1; the text renders as Markdown. |
| Closed but unreadable frontmatter | Invalid YAML (`frontmatter.yaml`) or a value that is not a mapping (`frontmatter.type`) is a warning at line 1; the block is removed from the body and the report renders without frontmatter. |
| Body | CommonMark plus the extensions in T-MARKDOWN-EXT. |
| Rich fence | A fenced code block whose trimmed, lowercased info string is a rich tag (T-RICH-FENCE). Its body is a YAML mapping decoded by that tag's schema. |
| Failed fence | Stays visible as a code block, with an `error` diagnostic at its line. |
| Other fences | Ordinary code blocks. |

The placeholders that splice rendered blocks into the Markdown are internal and not part of the format.

sources.label: Parse order, size limit, BOM, frontmatter and fence decoding
Only unclosed frontmatter falls back to Markdown; closed invalid or non-mapping frontmatter warns at line 1 and is cut from the body (`content = &source[after..]`), confirmed by probes

items.title: YAML profile
items.question: Which YAML features do frontmatter, rich fences and style files accept, and what happens to duplicate keys, anchors and non-finite numbers?
items.why: Today the parser library decides silently: a duplicated key keeps the last value, `.inf` becomes null, `0x10` becomes 16 and `0b11` becomes 3, so two readers of the same source can disagree on what it says.
items.proposed:
All RichView YAML (frontmatter, rich fences, `.rstyle.yaml`) uses one RichView profile: the YAML 1.2 core schema with the deviations and limits below.

| Construct | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Duplicate key in one mapping | Error `yaml.duplicate-key` at the second key's line |
| Anchors, aliases, merge keys, explicit tags | Error `yaml.unsupported` |
| `.inf`, `.nan` | Error; numbers are finite |
| `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, unquoted dates, `1_000`, `0b11` | Strings |
| `007` and other integers with a leading zero | Strings. Deviation: the 1.2 core schema reads `007` as 7; the profile keeps today's string |
| `0x10`, `0o17`, `1e3` | Numbers |
| `~`, `null` | Null |

Values that change meaning against today: `0b11` (3 today, a string under the profile), `.inf` and `.nan` (null today, an error), duplicate keys and anchors (accepted today, errors). The parser is a maintained YAML 1.2 implementation configured to this profile; `serde_yaml 0.9.34+deprecated` is not carried into the rewrite.

options.label: Strict RichView profile
options.detail: One meaning per source; an agent gets an error with a line instead of a silent overwrite. Leading-zero integers stay strings, as today.

options.label: Parser defaults (current)
options.detail: No work, but behaviour changes with the library and duplicate keys stay silent.

options.label: Strict profile with anchors allowed
options.detail: Keeps repeated chart styles short; aliases reopen expansion bombs and complicate line mapping.

items.recommendation: Strict RichView profile: agents write YAML fresh each time, so anchors buy little, while silent last-key-wins edits are exactly what an exact format must exclude.

sources.label: Duplicate `title` keys keep the second value; `.inf` becomes null; `0x10` becomes 16; anchors and aliases resolve; `yes` and unquoted dates stay strings (reproduced with the b4db233 release build)
Inline table probe decodes `007` as "007", `0b11` as 3, `0x10` as 16, `1_000` as "1_000", `0o17` as 15, `1e3` as 1000.0 and `.inf` as null (b4db233 release build)
YAML 1.2.2 core schema: integers `[-+]?[0-9]+`, `0o` octal and `0x` hex only

items.title: Format version marker
items.question: Should a report declare the format version it was written for, and if so where: in frontmatter (`format: rmd/1`), or only in the stored version's metadata as the June plan placed it?
items.why: The rewrite renames fields (`big`, `suffix`, chart style keys, header-image aliases). No b4db233 source carries a marker, so a marker cannot protect today's corpus unless absence means legacy; that corpus is protected only if INT-51 keeps existing sources working, by the rename errors and the automatic migration of D-TYP-MIGRATIONS. A marker matters for later breaking changes: it lets a renderer refuse a source written for a newer format. dec-9 said to re-promote the marker "when a real grammar break is on the roadmap", which the rewrite is.
items.proposed: Frontmatter may carry `format: rmd/1`; absent means the current major version. Every retired name keeps an error that names its replacement (D-TYP-MIGRATIONS), so an unmarked older source fails loudly instead of changing meaning; the automatic migration writes `format: rmd/1` into each source it rewrites. A renderer rejects a higher major version with `frontmatter.format` (error). Additive fields keep the version; renames and removals bump it. Rendered HTML carries `<meta name="generator" content="richview rmd/1">`, and the stored version's metadata records the format.

options.label: Absent means legacy

options.label: No marker
options.detail: Simplest; every later rename relies on retired-name diagnostics alone.

items.title: Frontmatter `slides` and its diagnostics
items.question: Is one boolean frontmatter field the whole syntax of slides?

items.question: May a report name its own background, or turn a preset's default off, without a style file?

items.title: Unknown keys and invalid values in blocks
items.question: What happens to a block key the schema does not know, and to a known key whose value breaks its rule?
items.why: Today unknown keys pass silently in the CLI, MCP and server, are copied into the chart runtime payload, and warn only in VS Code; histogram `binning` alone rejects them. A known key whose value breaks its type, enum or range is `block.schema` (error): the fence stays visible as code and publish refuses the report. Presentation fields get no exception.

items.title: Value formats
items.question: Should tables, metrics and axes share one `format` vocabulary and one `unit` rule?
items.why: Axes implement only `percent` and `currency`, tables and metrics five names, unknown names render raw text silently, and grouping is always English. Axes also rescale a few named units (`K`, `M`, `KBD`) that tables print literally.
items.proposed:
One vocabulary for table columns, metrics and `axes.*.format`. Every number is rounded to a precision in significant digits: three by default and four at most, with a scale word for large values (FEA-CH-37). `digits` on a chart, an axis, a table column or a metric sets it; a chart's `readout_digits` sets its readouts, Table and CSV, and may exceed its labels. Readers never see more digits than these allow, anywhere.

| `format` | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `number` | Grouped, never scaled (`1,234`) |
| `number_compact` | Scale word: `167 thousand`, `1.23 million`; K, M, B on axes (FEA-CH-22) |
| `percent` | ×100, `%` |
| `year` | Integer without grouping; only if part 04a keeps it (FEA-CH-21, OPN-11) |
| absent | Numbers: `number` below 10,000, `number_compact` from 10,000; text as written; axes: automatic labelling (part 04a) |

`unit` exists on columns, metrics and axes with one rule: a unit that is or ends in a currency symbol (`$`, `US$`, `€`, `£`, `¥`) leads the value, any other unit follows it (`12 users`, `1 234 Kč`); `percent` prints its own `%` once. On axes the magnitude units `k` or `K`, `M` and `KBD` scale up once when values reach 1,000 (`K` reads `M`, `M` reads `B`, `KBD` reads `MBD`, as FEA-CH-23 describes); every other unit stays literal. Separators follow `lang`. An unknown name is `block.schema`. Money formats: D-TYP-CURRENCY.

items.title: Unused data columns in reports
items.question: Should a report embed only the fields its blocks reference, or every column of each referenced dataset?
items.why: Every column ships today: an unused `secret_note` CSV column appears in the report HTML, the engine builds chart readouts from every field of a row, and the CSV file is copied to `Rendered/data/`. An author who charts two columns of a wide export publishes all of them. Projection has a cost for readers: readouts lose context fields such as names or notes, and the chart's CSV download no longer gives the full dataset. It protects only the HTML file: on a RichView server `/raw/` serves the source with its inline data, and today's bundle route returns every stored file (T-STORED-REPORT and FEA-SF-15 decide that route).
items.proposed: Each chart embeds only the fields its `encoding`, `facet` and annotations reference, plus the fields listed in `encoding.detail`; a table embeds its `columns`, or every column when `columns` is absent. Chart readouts, Table views and CSV downloads show those fields for all rows. Core computes every position, statistic and aggregate from the exact source values before it writes the report: bins, densities, quartiles, flows, order, stack totals, scales and layout. The HTML never holds the exact values. It holds three things. **Shown values:** every observation carries its value as shown, at the most precise setting the author shows for that block (FEA-CH-37), keyed by the mark's identity (panel, series, x). Every readout, label, legend, Table cell, CSV cell and accessible name is formatted from the shown value, never from a position, so the text is exactly what the author chose; there is no per-state text. **Positions:** every channel that places a mark is embedded on a grid of its own scale, over that scale's domain, never zero to the maximum. The grid has 4,096 steps, or as many steps as the author's shown precision distinguishes across the domain, whichever is more, and never more: a step is never finer than both the author's last shown digit and 1/4,096 of the domain. Zoom stops where one grid step spans about two pixels at the chart's width, so a zoomable chart can be zoomed as deep as the author's precision supports and no deeper. Dates and integers use the data's own resolution. The chart engine declares which channels share a scale. A position therefore never yields more digits than the author shows or the default view draws. **Derived structure:** statistics and structure (bins, densities, quartiles, flows, order, totals) come from core's layout and are embedded once for the initial state and once for each discrete state of a control the author defines. Interactions that only filter or zoom, such as a legend toggle or a zoom, never recompute them: they hide or clip embedded marks. A total the browser must compute after such an interaction is the sum of shown values, formatted at the author's precision, which a reader could already compute from the Table. The payload grows linearly with the data and the author's states, and every number a reader can see or retrieve is one the author's precision allows. Data files are not copied into `Rendered/` (T-RENDERED-OUTPUT). Columns of a data file that no block references never reach the HTML; inline data stays visible in the published source.

options.detail: Unreferenced columns never ship; `encoding.detail: [name, note]` keeps chosen context in readouts, Table views and downloads; one more channel to learn.

items.recommendation: Referenced fields plus `encoding.detail`: the author decides which context readers see, and a wide export never ships whole by accident.

items.title: CSV typing rules
items.question: Are these the CSV rules, including comma-only delimiters and text kept wherever a number would lose precision?
items.why: CSV typing decides what charts plot and how tables sort; a wrong guess turns identifiers into numbers or rounds values.
items.proposed:
| Input | Result |
| --- | --- |
| File | UTF-8, BOM dropped, RFC 4180 quoting, comma delimiter |
| Cells | Every header and value is trimmed of surrounding whitespace |
| Header | First row; names non-empty and unique, else `data.csv.header` |
| Ragged row | `data.csv` with the file line |
| Empty cell | null |
| `true`, `false` | booleans |
| Number whose decimal value survives binary64 (`1.5`, `-3`, `10.50`) | number (`10.50` becomes 10.5) |
| Token with a leading zero (`00123`; not `0` or `0.5`) | string identifier: sorted as text and never totalled, so its column gets no total |
| Integer beyond 2^53, or decimal that does not round-trip | numeric text: kept as written, sorted by exact decimal value, totalled in binary64 |
| Missing markers (`n/a`, `NA`, `.`) | D-TYP-MISSING-VALUE |
| Anything else | string |

"Kept as written" governs parsing, sorting and totals only; readers see every number at the author's precision (FEA-CH-37). There is no `delimiter` option; a semicolon file fails as ragged rows or as missing fields (D-TYP-FIELD-CHECKS).

items.title: Parquet data files
items.question: Does a block read a Parquet file in the report folder through `data.parquet`, parsed only in the confined SQL worker, with only the columns the report uses read, and with SQL over the same file as the way to aggregate it?
items.why: Daniel asked on 9 November 2026 for "Parquet data files for large data, and smaller reports with many charts". A report's size follows the rows each chart draws, not the file's format: eight all-row charts over one 100,000-row, 10.5 MB CSV made a 34.2 MB HTML file in 6.7 s (docs/lockdown/evidence/parquet.md). A wide export read as CSV is parsed whole and capped at 16 MiB of file. Parquet lets one large file stay in the folder, costs only the columns a report reads, and SQL over it gives each chart its own few aggregated rows.
items.proposed:
| Rule | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Key | `data.parquet`: a report-relative path, under the report-folder rules of T-REPORT-FOLDER; one of the block's exclusive sources (TYP-35) |
| Reader | DuckDB's Parquet reader inside the confined SQL worker (FEA-BR-14's sandbox): the worker reads that one file and nothing else, reaches no network and writes nowhere; 30 s and 256 MiB. Core never receives Parquet bytes (ARC-02) |
| Hosts | Native hosts only: the `richview` command and RichView servers. A browser host reports `data.unresolved` naming them. On Linux the worker needs kernel 6.2 or newer, as SQL sources do |
| Columns | Only the columns the report's blocks name in that file are read, once per render for every block that names it: a chart's fields (TYP-36), a table's `columns`, or every column for a table without them. Other columns are never read and never reach the HTML |
| Rows | Every row, never a sample |
| Types | Parquet's types decide. Integers and floats are numbers; a decimal is a number read from its own digits, not through a nearest float, and its trailing zeros are not kept (TYP-104); a decimal or integer binary64 cannot hold is numeric text (TYP-37); text stays text, so `00123` or `123` stored as text never becomes a number; booleans are booleans; dates, times and timestamps become ISO 8601 text; nulls are missing |
| NaN and infinities | Missing, with one `data.parquet.non-finite` warning per column giving the count |
| Unsupported column | A list, struct, map, union, interval or binary column that a block reads is `data.parquet` (error) naming the column and its kind |
| Unreadable file | Not Parquet, truncated, damaged or encrypted: `data.parquet` (error) at each block that names it, with no engine text |
| Limits | At most 1,000,000 rows from one file, and the columns read stay under TYP-43's 16 MiB dataset limit: `data.limit`, whose fix names SQL. The file itself may be larger; on Windows the worker reads a private copy of at most 4 GiB |
| Aggregation | Report SQL over the same file through the connector route (TYP-35, TYP-79, FEA-BR-14): a connector of kind `parquet` in `report.connectors.yaml` names the file with `file`, and `data.sql` reads it as the table named after the connector. The read-only guard, bound parameters, the 100,000-row cap, snapshots and the provenance finding apply unchanged. A snapshot follows the file: a file written again is queried again |

No author text reaches SQL for a `data.parquet` block: the host writes the query, and column names are taken from the file's own schema after an exact match with the texts of the blocks that name it. A statistic chart over every row still embeds every row (TYP-36); TYP-103 proposes the alternative.

options.detail: A hostile file is parsed inside the operating system's sandbox, the same engine serves SQL over the file, and only the worker binary grows. Costs the Linux kernel 6.2 requirement that SQL sources already have.

options.label: A pure Rust reader in the resolver
options.detail: No kernel requirement and no worker; a hostile file is parsed in the command and server process, a second Parquet implementation sits beside DuckDB's, and SQL over the file still needs the worker.

options.label: No Parquet
options.detail: Authors export one CSV per chart, as today; a wide or large export never sits in the report folder as one file.

items.recommendation: Confined worker with DuckDB's Parquet reader: it is the only option that parses a hostile file outside the host process, and it adds one Cargo feature to an engine the worker already links.
items.conflicts: INT-24 keeps RichView out of computing metrics: this card adds no aggregation vocabulary; aggregation is the author's SQL through the connector route OPN-63 already decides. TYP-35's "exactly one of" list and TYP-43's dataset limit gain a Parquet row each. ARC-27 keeps the editor, build and bench free of connector engines: the editor service resolves through the same host code and has no worker beside it, so a `data.parquet` block there reports that the worker is missing; whether the editor ships the worker is open. A file on a Linux kernel older than 6.2 is not read; the lead accepted that on 19 November 2026 in place of a second reader.

For a statistic chart over a large file the observations are most of the report and none of the picture: on a 100,000-row file a histogram's payload is 1.31 MB of which its 30 bins are about 2 KB, a box plot's is 3.07 MB and a density's 0.84 MB (docs/lockdown/evidence/parquet.md). Below the count nothing changes. Charts whose marks are observations (scatter, line, strip, dot plot) are untouched; their per-point readout text is the readout-numbers payload work.

items.title: A column from a typed numeric source shows one number of decimals
items.question: Should a field from a typed numeric source be shown with one number of decimals across its column, decided by the author or by the source's declared scale?
items.why: A value that arrives as a number has no written form, so its trailing zeros are gone. A SQL result or a Parquet column that holds 9.26, 9.00 and 8.98 prints 9.26, 9 and 8.98 in a heatmap, and a table prints 7% among 6.1%. A CSV does the same: `9.00` written in a file prints 9 (checked on the release build of 19 November 2026). The vocabulary sets significant digits (`digits`) and has no way to fix decimal places, so an author cannot repair it. The Parquet example printed it on every page until its queries were changed to return whole numbers and one-decimal averages (the lead's review of 19 November 2026).
items.proposed:
Not built.

| Rule | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | A field whose values arrive typed as numbers: a `data.sql` result, a `data.parquet` column, a JSON number. Whether a CSV column follows the same rule, with the most decimals written in the column as its declared scale, is part of this question |
| One scale per column | Every printed value of the field, in a chart's labels and readouts and in a table's cells, shows the same number of decimals |
| The author decides | A new closed option beside `digits`, a whole number of decimal places from 0 to 6, on a chart, an axis and a table column |
| Else the source's declared scale | A column the source declares with a fixed scale, such as SQL or Parquet `DECIMAL(12,2)`, shows that scale: 9.00 stays 9.00. The worker passes the scale with the column |
| Else the data | A column of floats with no declared scale shows the most decimals any of its values needs within the author's significant digits, on every row |
| Never more than the author chose | The scale never shows a digit beyond the author's `digits` or decimals (FEA-CH-37): padding adds zeros, never precision |
| Whole numbers | A column whose values are all whole shows no decimals, as today |

options.label: One scale per column, from the author or the source
options.detail: A typed column reads as a column: 9.26, 9.00, 8.98. Adds one option to the vocabulary and a scale to the rows a host passes for SQL and Parquet.

options.label: Keep today's shortest form per value
options.detail: No change to the vocabulary or the payload; a typed column mixes 9 and 9.26, and the author works around it in SQL by returning whole numbers.

items.recommendation: One scale per column, from the author or the source: a column of measurements is read down, and mixed decimals read as different precision that the data does not have.
items.conflicts: FEA-CH-37 bounds what readers see by the author's precision; this card pads with zeros and never adds a digit. TYP-37 types a CSV cell from its text, and its trailing zeros are lost when the cell becomes a number, so the same reader sees the same mix from a CSV. `digits` stays significant digits; whether the new option may stand beside `digits` on one field or replaces it there is open. The lead ruled on 19 November 2026 that this is proposed and the engine change is not built that night.

items.title: Date and time values
items.question: Which strings count as dates and times, and with what precision?
items.why: T-CHART-ENCODING puts line and area charts on a calendar axis when every `x` is a date string, and calendar ticks, readouts and annotations follow the precision. Today the engine's `parse_iso` decides which forms count; no document states them.
items.proposed:
| Form | Example | Precision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `YYYY` | `2020` | Year |
| `YYYY-MM` | `2020-03` | Month |
| `YYYY-MM-DD` | `2020-03-31` | Day |
| Date, then `T`, `t` or a space, then `HH:MM` | `2020-03-31T14:05` | Minute |
| The same with `:SS` | `2020-03-31 14:05:09` | Second |
| The same with a fraction of 1 to 9 digits after `.` or `,` | `2020-03-31T14:05:09.5` | Millisecond; digits beyond three are dropped |

A date-time may end in `Z` or `z`, `±HH`, `±HHMM` or `±HH:MM`; without an offset it is UTC. Surrounding spaces are ignored. Out-of-range fields (month 13, 30 February, 25:00, an offset of 24 hours) make the value a non-date. Only strings qualify: a quoted year is temporal, an unquoted year a number. An axis is calendar only when every `x` value qualifies, so one missing or malformed `x` turns it into a numeric or category axis. These are today's rules.

sources.label: `parse_iso`: accepted forms, offsets, range checks, precision

items.title: Missing values and numeric text
items.question: Which cell values mean missing, and do tables and every chart read them the same way?
items.why: The time-series engine treats empty, `.`, `na`, `n/a`, `nan`, `null` and `none` (any case) as missing and rejects comma-grouped numbers; other charts turn every non-numeric cell into a gap with one warning; tables keep all of them as text. The same CSV cell is therefore a gap, a warning or an error depending on the chart: a bar chart with `n/a`, `1,234` and `NA` warns `chart.non-numeric-y` ("3 nonnumeric observations render as gaps"), while a calendar line fails on `1,234` with `chart.source-error`.
items.proposed: One rule for inline, CSV and JSON data in every block. A missing value is null, an empty CSV cell, or `.`, `NA`, `N/A`, `NaN`, `null` or `none` in any case after trimming. Charts draw it as a gap (FEA-CH-38) and count it in their diagnostics. Tables print the cell as written, sort it after every value and leave it out of totals. Any other text in a numeric chart channel, including comma-grouped numbers such as `1,234`, is `chart.non-numeric` (error) naming the row and value; in a table it stays text.

options.label: Markers are gaps, other text is an error
options.detail: One rule for every chart; a misformatted number can never vanish from a chart silently.

options.label: Every non-numeric cell is a gap with a warning
options.detail: Today's rule outside calendar charts; drafts always render, and a `1,234` cell disappears with a warning.

options.label: Only null and empty cells are missing
options.detail: Strictest; exports that write `n/a` fail until cleaned.

items.recommendation: Markers are gaps, other text is an error: missing data stays visible as missing (FEA-CH-38), and a wrong number fails where an agent sees it.

items.title: Report folder and path rules
items.question: Is the report folder contract (one `.rmd` per folder, report-relative paths only, no network) the rule for every host?
items.why: It decides what a report may reference and makes renders reproducible; today `--allow-network` is accepted and ignored, which advertises a capability that does not exist.
items.proposed: A report is one folder with exactly one `.rmd`; subfolders are allowed. Every referenced file (data, styles, media, posters, header image, Markdown images and relative links) is a report-relative path: non-empty, no leading `/`, no `..`, `\`, `:`, `?`, `#`, `%` or NUL, resolving without symlinks to a regular file inside the folder. Escape is `report.asset.escape` and absence `report.asset.missing`, both at the referencing line with report-relative paths in the message. A missing, shared or escaping root fails fast (`report.root.*`). Resolution never uses the network; `--allow-network` is removed.

items.title: Remote images, audio and video
items.question: May a report reference media by plain URL, or must every image, audio and video file live in the report folder or behind a pinned asset reference?
items.why: Any `https://` media `src` or Markdown image fails the whole render today with `report.asset.escape` and an absolute-path message, while the spec says remote assets are diagnosed and mark the report as not offline.
items.proposed: Report-local or pinned. Every image, audio file, video, poster and header image comes from the report folder or, now that Daniel's INT-31 answer brings uploads and hosted assets into the rewrite, from a pinned asset reference (TYP-41) on RichView's managed hosting or the author's own host. A plain remote media `src`, poster, header image or Markdown image is `report.asset.remote` (error) at its line, telling the author to download the file into the folder or upload it as a pinned reference. The one exception is an `images.unsplash.com` photo on an image block or `title_image` with a `credit`, which is hotlinked as Daniel's FEA-RP-62 answer accepts; without a credit it warns. Only that element is dropped (a Markdown image shows its alt text), so the draft stays viewable; publish refuses the report. Renders never fetch a pinned asset; they read its verified local copy (ARC-11, TYP-41). Besides hotlinked Unsplash photos, `embed` is the only remote content that is not pinned.

items.title: Pinned remote asset references
items.question: Do `src` and `data` accept integrity-pinned remote asset references (`url`, `bytes`, `sha256`, `type`, `visibility`), the hosting contract S27-616 asks for, in the form below?
items.why: S27-616 (2026-10-10) asks for externally hosted large datasets, video, pictures and audio "so authors do not have to embed large payloads inside reports", with a clear asset reference and loading contract. The `AssetRef` type and the upload commands exist (PR #22), but no `.rmd` field accepts a reference, so nothing consumes them. ARC-34 decides the uploader commands and MCP tools; this card decides only the source type.
items.proposed:
In the rewrite (INT-31): besides report-relative paths and `data:` URIs (T-REPORT-FOLDER), `src` and `data` accept an `AssetRef` mapping as PR #22's type defines it: `url` (HTTPS), `bytes`, `sha256` (lowercase hex of the whole object), `type` (a media type from each use's allowlist), `visibility` (`public` or `private`), and optional `duration` (audio and video) and `width` and `height` (image and video, to reserve layout). `url` points at RichView's managed hosting (INT-27) or the author's own HTTPS host or S3-compatible bucket; a presigned URL is never a reference. Renders and checks never fetch (ARC-11): they read a verified local copy that the upload keeps (ARC-34, FEA-SF-50), and an explicit download command fetches a missing copy and checks its size and SHA-256; a missing or mismatched copy is an error at the field's line. The published page links the asset and the reader's browser loads it from its host; the runtime checks a dataset's SHA-256 before use. A plain remote URL stays an error (TYP-40).

Open: what the self-contained file and the PDF hold for a hosted asset (TYP-42); how a private asset reaches its readers, since a presigned URL is never a reference; and where the verified local copy lives (inside the report folder and ignored by Git, or a user cache).

options.detail: Daniel's INT-31 answer: large data and media live on RichView's managed hosting or the author's own host; the rewrite defines the verified local copy, credentials for private assets and what the self-contained HTML holds.

options.label: Defer with ARC-34
options.detail: The earlier proposal: no source field accepts a reference in the first cut; contradicts INT-31, which brings uploads and hosted assets into the rewrite.

items.recommendation: Wire AssetRef into `src` and `data`: Daniel's INT-31 answer brings uploads, author-hosted assets and RichView-managed hosting into the rewrite, and pinning by size and SHA-256 keeps published reports verifiable while their bytes live elsewhere.

items.title: Rendered output
items.question: Is `Rendered/<basename>.html`, self-contained, the output contract of every local render and export?
items.why: Agents and Daniel verify the generated file itself (G-ARTIFACT-PROOF, enforced by G-BUILD in DEL-13), so its location and contents must be predictable. Today export also copies every referenced data, style and media file beside the HTML that already embeds them.
items.proposed: Native renders write `Rendered/<source basename>.html` (or `.pdf`) inside the report folder; `-o` names another file directly in `Rendered/`. A symlinked, escaping or colliding target is `report.output.*` (error). The HTML is self-contained: styles, fonts, data, local media and the chart runtime are inline, so it opens offline from any location. This holds for every local render and export; the one variant is the report host's hosted page, which links the runtime and fonts from content-hashed routes on that host and offers this file as a download (INT-04, ARC-07, ARC-24, TYP-70). Assets referenced through pinned asset references (TYP-41) are the other exception: the page links them and the reader's browser loads them from their host, so they are not inline. Open: what the self-contained file and the PDF hold for a hosted asset: a link, a poster or placeholder, or the bytes embedded when under a size limit. A photo hotlinked from Unsplash (FEA-RP-62) is the same kind of exception: the file shows it only online, and what an offline file and the PDF show for it is open. Only files that relative Markdown links point to are copied beside it, with the same relative paths.

items.title: Size and count limits
items.question: Are these the limits, enforced the same way in every host, and can every report that renders also be published?
items.why: Limits protect hosts from oversized input and set the ceiling for embedded media. Today they do not fit together: up to 64 MiB of resolved resources renders locally, but publishing sends them in a request body capped at 32 MiB, and T-PUBLISH-REQUEST sends binary files as base64, which adds a third. PRF-62's informational fixture (about 16 MB of CSV, roughly 15 MiB) sits just under the 16 MiB dataset limit.
items.proposed:
| Limit | Value | On breach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.rmd` source | 16 MiB | `source.limit` |
| One resolved dataset | 16 MiB | `data.limit` |
| One Parquet file's rows | 1,000,000, and the 16 MiB above counted on the columns the report reads, not on the file (TYP-102) | `data.limit` |
| Resolved data, media and styles together | 64 MiB | error naming the largest files |
| Report HTML | 64 MiB | `render.output-limit` |
| HTTP render and MCP request body, host file read | 32 MiB | error |
| Publish request body | Change: 104 MiB, enough for 64 MiB of files as base64 plus a 16 MiB source | error |
| Editor service request | 24 MiB | error |
| Entries in a report folder, files and directories alike | 10,000 | `report.root.unresolved` |
| Chart width | D-TYP-WIDTH-RANGE | `options.width` |

PRF-62's fixture must stay under the dataset limit; a larger fixture needs that limit raised first.

items.title: Style file structure and merge
items.question: Is a `.rstyle.yaml` five sections merged leaf by leaf, with one invalid leaf skipping only itself rather than the whole file?
items.why: One unknown token skips the entire file today, so a typo silently drops every valid value with a warning that has no line; unknown sections are ignored without notice. The June plan went the strict way: dec-18 rejected unknown leaves under `tokens`, `layout` and `chart` with an error and let only unknown top-level sections degrade.
items.proposed: A style file is a YAML mapping with optional sections `tokens`, `layout`, `chart`, `motion` and `components`. Styles apply in order (frontmatter `styles`, then CLI `--style`); later files win per leaf and lists replace. An unknown section or leaf is `style.unknown-key` (warning); a value that breaks its grammar is `style.schema` (warning). Both skip only that leaf and carry the style file's path and line. Retired leaves are unknown keys. Keys that fix the page's mechanics, such as `measure` and `report-max-width`, are set only by builtins: in an author's file they are `style.internal` (warning) and skip like a bad leaf (OPN-59). Every author-facing key carries a `safe` or `experimental` mark in the registry (Daniel's STY-14 answer), shown by `richview learn`, the docs and editor completions; the mark guides agents and never changes validation.

options.label: Skip only the bad leaf
options.detail: The rest of the style applies and the warning says exactly where; a typo can reach a published report as a small visual difference.

options.label: Error on unknown leaves (dec-18)
options.detail: An unknown leaf is `style.unknown-key` (error) and publish refuses the report; unknown sections warn. The closed vocabulary is enforced mechanically; drafts still render without the leaf.

options.label: Skip the whole file (current)
options.detail: Never applies half a design; one typo loses the file.

options.label: Fail the render
options.detail: Loudest; blocks drafts over a colour typo.

items.recommendation: Skip only the bad leaf: styles cascade, so one stray leaf should not cost the rest of a shared style, and the warning carries the line. Choose dec-18's error if published reports must never differ from their style by a typo.

items.question: Are these the tokens, and the closed grammars every CSS-bound style value must match?
items.why: The grammars are the security boundary between style files and the page's CSS; the token list is what part 06's builtins set.

items.title: Style values reaching CSS unchecked
items.question: How does the rewrite guarantee that no style value can break out of CSS into HTML, and does the sink serializer refuse or escape a bad value?
items.why: Reproduced on 2026-10-21: with `styles: [sleek, report.rstyle.yaml]` and a `chart.palette` entry `red;}</style><script>alert(1)</script><style>{`, generate returns `ok: true` with no style diagnostic and the report contains a live `<script>`. items.title: What makes two publications the same content
items.question: Which bytes decide whether a republished version is identical: the `.rmd` source alone, or the whole publish request?
items.why: D-TYP-REPUBLISH and the stored `contentSha256` depend on it. Today `content_sha256` hashes only the `.rmd` source, so a republish that changes only a CSV, a style file or an image counts as identical. dec-67 defined a version as source plus snapshotted styles, rendered HTML and metadata, and ARC-21 says "identical source and resources".
items.proposed: `contentSha256` is the SHA-256 of the canonical publish request: the `.rmd` source bytes, the ordered style references, and every entry of `files` sorted by report-relative path, each as its path, byte length and bytes. Slug and version are not part of it, and neither are the rendered HTML or the engine version, so re-rendering never changes identity. Two publications of one `{slug, version}` are identical exactly when their hashes match.

items.title: Republishing an existing version

items.title: Which version is latest

items.title: Version retention
items.question: Are published versions kept forever, or pruned at 50 per slug as today?
items.why: After 52 publications, 0.0.1 and 0.0.2 return 404 although versioned pages are served `immutable, max-age=31536000`; the pruned 0.0.1 could then be published again with different content and became latest, pruning 0.0.3. The cap is the June plan, not drift: the architecture page specified at most 50 versions per slug, the oldest pruned on the 51st publish, each prune logged and the cap configurable by an environment variable, as the mitigation for the storage cost of immutability. The code has the cap (`MAX_VERSIONS = 50`) without the variable or the logging.
items.proposed: Published versions are never deleted automatically (ARC-21). A per-deployment storage quota in bytes, set in the server's configuration, bounds growth; a publication that would exceed it is `publish.quota` (error, HTTP 507) and nothing is stored. Deleting a version is an explicit authenticated request (`DELETE /api/reports/{slug}/v/{version}`, T-HTTP-API) that leaves a tombstone: its permalink returns 410 and that `{slug, version}` can never be published again.

options.label: 50-version cap (June plan)
options.detail: As planned: prune the oldest on the 51st publish, log each prune, cap set by an environment variable; old permalinks disappear, and a tombstone is still needed so a pruned version cannot return with different content.

items.recommendation: Permanent, with quota and tombstones: a permalink served as immutable must not 404 after 50 later publishes.

items.title: MCP tool contracts
items.question: Do MCP report tools take a report path and return the CLI's JSON, with typed inputs for every tool and `isError` reserved for calls that could not run?
items.why: A source-only `richview_validate` fails with `report.root.missing` today, `richview_render` needs `input_path` to write anything, and `isError` is set whenever a diagnostic is an error, so clients treat "your chart has a problem" like a failed tool call. items.proposed: Report tools (`richview_validate`, `richview_check`, `richview_render`, `richview_publish`) take `inputPath` to a `.rmd` in its report folder plus the CLI's options (`theme`, `styles`, `chartWidth`, `output`, `page`, `publish`, `server`, `slug`). There is no `token` argument: publishing uses the token from the MCP host's environment (ARC-23, FEA-SF-12). `richview_learn` takes an optional `section`, one of `grammar`, `chart-contract`, `style`, `workflow` or `anti-slop`, and returns text generated from the schema registry that the renderer uses (Daniel's INT-21 answer, INT-66). Every diagnostic a report tool returns carries its line and a `fix` (TYP-53), so an agent can repair an error from one result. Tool annotations stay as today: `richview_learn`, `richview_validate` and `richview_check` are read-only; every tool except `richview_render` is idempotent; only `richview_publish` reaches the network; none is destructive. Report tools return the T-CLI-JSON object as `structuredContent` and a one-line summary as text. `isError` is true only when the call could not run (bad arguments, unreadable folder, network failure); a report with errors returns `ok: false` and `isError: false`. Which tools exist is D-MCP-SURFACE (part 04c); the two image tools' contracts follow FEA-RP-62 (OPN-67); resources and protocol negotiation are FEA-SF-11 and FEA-SF-10. Server-side MCP (a RichView server exposing MCP to an agent, which INT-25 allows at most) may come later and is not part of the rewrite; the rewrite ships stdio MCP only.

A line or area recedes by series (one without a matching row), a bar, lollipop or scatter point by row. A highlight that matches no row mutes nothing.

items.title: Data connectors (PR #66)
items.question: If Publish's live-data path needs reports to name their live source, are PR #66's `data.sql`, `data.metricflow` and `data.cache` the types to add, or does the core format stay unchanged?
items.why: Daniel's INT-24 answer keeps exported data the default for every report and puts live connections in RichView Publish, behind a third-party connector engine. Any key that names a live source in `.rmd` reverses today's `data.sql` error and makes a render depend on connectors configured outside the report, so the core format should change only if Publish cannot bind live data without it.
items.proposed:
Reports name their live source: a block's `data` may be `sql` against a connector the RichView server offers, in place of a CSV or JSON file (OPN-63). Connectors are standard on every RichView server, Cowork and Publish, local and hosted; RichView builds the connector core and PR #66's work enters it, so its keys are the starting shape:

| Key | Type | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data.sql` | `{connector, query}` or `{connector, inline}` | `query` is a report-relative `.sql` file, `inline` SQL text; exactly one |
| `data.metricflow` | `{connector, metrics}` | Non-empty list of metric names; only if the agents keep MetricFlow (FEA-BR-15) |
| `data.cache` | `{key}` | Snapshot key; published renders read the snapshot, never the connector |

A RichView server with that connector resolves the query and stores a snapshot (FEA-BR-16); anywhere else the block is `data.unresolved`. A self-contained HTML file never queries live data (OPN-63). Connectors are named in the server's configuration, named people manage them and access is granted per person (FEA-SF-19); credentials stay in the server's configuration, never in the report, its output, MCP arguments or agent context (ARC-23). `data` still has exactly one source key. The final key names, and whether the CLI resolves `sql` itself or only through a local RichView server, are the agents' technical choice (OPN-63).

items.title: Publication metadata (PR #70)
items.question: Now that the rewrite builds RichView Publish (INT-31, INT-35), does its `publish:` frontmatter mapping become part of the `.rmd` format?
items.why: It adds 16 fields, a second slug beside the top-level `slug`, and dashboard snapshots; news.richview.ai already runs it from #70's code, merged into `main` as it is on 2026-10-26 (97ac0d0, INT-52).
items.proposed: Adopt as an optional namespace: `publish: {id, slug, summary (≤600), byline (≤160), section, tags, published, updated (RFC 3339), state (draft/published/hidden), audience, kind (report/page), aliases, corrections [{date, note}], cover, cover_alt, cover_credit (required when `cover` is a hotlinked Unsplash URL, FEA-RP-62)}` as PR #70 defines it; `kind: dashboard` and `snapshot` follow FEA-BR-30 (OPN-67). Ids and slugs follow the T-REPORT-SLUG grammar. Core validates the mapping, so every host reports the same diagnostics; only Publish acts on it, and Cowork and local renders ignore it. News's items keep their metadata when News moves onto the rewrite's Publish (INT-74, INT-51). Open: whether `publish.slug` replaces the top-level `slug`, as #70 has it, or both may coexist, since Cowork addresses reports by the top-level slug (FEA-SF-14) and the same source may be published to both servers.

options.label: Adopt as an optional namespace

items.title: Publication `site.yaml` (PR #70)
items.question: Is PR #70's `site.yaml` the site configuration type of the rewrite's Publish?
items.why: It is a third YAML file type beside `.rmd` and `.rstyle.yaml`, with its own `theme` and `accent` separate from the style cascade.
items.proposed: Adopt with T-PUBLISH-META, as the configuration of one Publish publication: `title`, `description`, `base_url`, `layout` (`broadsheet`/`dispatch`), `mode` (`external`/`internal`; `internal` only if FEA-BR-45 keeps it), `theme` (`paper`/`ink`), `accent` (six-digit hex), `sections` (≤20 `{id, title, description}`), `navigation` (≤12 `{label, path}`), `lead` (≤4 ids). Unknown keys fail validation. Rows follow FEA-BR-23 and FEA-BR-45 once they are answered (OPN-67).
